is the person's message, delivered, and the client hides a Queued entry once its text was delivered.

feat: terminal and streaming never run at the same time; switch modes with resume; v0.106.37

- POST /api/agents/:id/runtime-mode stops the running mode, confirms it
  stopped, then starts the other resuming the agent's own conversation
  (claude --resume in tmux). Mode stored on the agent, not the browser.
- /stream-chat refuses while the terminal or an outside session runs; wake
  refuses while a stream runs; hibernate stops a stream; a per-agent start
  lock covers the same-instant race; restore and session create are guarded.
- "Outside tmux" now requires the Claude process the hook recorded to be
  alive (plugin 1.19.3), so a crash or reboot no longer hides an agent.
- The schedule runner wakes through wakeAgent instead of a bare `claude`,
  and sends into a live stream.

Merge pull request #736 from 23blocks-OS/fix/streaming-own-identity

fix: a streaming session has the agent's identity and resumes its own conversation; v0.106.36

fix: a streaming session has the agent's identity and resumes its own conversation; v0.106.36

The stream env set AIMAESTRO_AGENT_ID while the hook and AMP read AIM_AGENT_ID,
AIM_AGENT_NAME and AMP_DIR, so a stream session took its folder's identity.
It also resumed the newest JSONL in the folder, another agent's in a shared one.
Now it sets all three and resumes only the agent's claudeSessionId, never a
conversation live outside tmux or written to in the last 10 minutes.

fix: run the embedding model in a bounded child process (v0.83.3)

transformers.js / ONNX Runtime ran inside the server: native memory grew
and was never returned, Next could bundle embeddings.ts twice and load two
models, and inference blocked the event loop. On macOS the growth went to
compressed memory and swap, invisible to RSS, until the machine froze.

- lib/rag/embedding-worker.mjs is the only process that loads the model.
- lib/rag/embedding-client.mjs: one queue per server (on globalThis),
  two texts per request, timeout, crash/hang recovery, queue limits, and
  a replacement only after the old worker exits.

than to a job: it has a name, a memory that survives the session, an inbox, and

started would type the path at a shell that would try to execute it.

cannot be told, and calling that success would be the same unearned claim
removed everywhere else this cycle.

feat(amp): implement attachments; verify the program actually started (v0.38.0) (#442)

TRACK 1 — ATTACHMENTS

amp-send.sh --attach has been getting 404 since the flag shipped: the client
implemented the full flow, the endpoints were never built, and the skill
advertised it. An agent asked to send a file followed our own documentation
into a dead end.

Implemented against agentmessaging/protocol spec/attachment-guide.md v0.1.2,
so no client change is needed.

No S3, and the spec permits it: content is stored "externally by the
provider (e.g., in S3 OR EQUIVALENT object storage)". The client PUTs to
whatever URL it is handed, so a URL on this host is as conformant as a
presigned S3 one — and files stay inside the tailnet. Storage is
content-addressed by the sha256 the client already computes.

basic_clean, not clean: the spec provides a status for a provider that runs
the required checks and no AV, and requires it to declare av_scanning:false
in /v1/info. Returning `clean` would claim a scan we do not perform. The
client already understands it and prints "passed basic checks only (no AV
scan)" to the receiving agent.

All three MUST checks from section 5 (size+digest, blocked types, magic
bytes at primary-type level) apply to LOCAL delivery too — there is no
carve-out anywhere in the spec.

Download URLs carry a capability token, not an API key: the spec requires
cross-provider fetch without an account, and that URL travels inside a
message to another host.

Verified with the real client: --attach -> routed message -> --all ->
byte-identical file, digest checked in and out.

TRACK 2 — LAUNCH VERIFICATION

send-keys returning proves tmux took the keystrokes, not that the program
exists. An agent whose program is missing, unauthenticated or off PATH came
up looking healthy with a bare shell — #426, and the reason configuring an
uninstalled framework was indistinguishable from a working agent.

Measured, not predicted: a preflight `command -v` cannot reproduce the
pane's environment (tmux = interactive non-login, server check =
non-interactive), so it would disagree with the pane it describes. We look
at what happened and quote the shell's own diagnosis.

Any doubt counts as started — a false "did not start" is worse than silence.

Reported by @Shadercloud on a fresh install: created an agent, sent it a
sentence of English, and bash executed it —

  Steve: command not found
  Command 'The' not found, did you mean: command 'he' from deb node-he

Session status `online` means the TMUX SESSION EXISTS, not that an agent is
running in it. Chat and meeting injection checked only that, so a pane at a
shell prompt accepted the message and the shell ran it, one line at a time.

feat(companion): agents that look alive on a call, lips driven by the voice (v0.37.11) (#435)

The call screen had a static portrait and a five-bar "waveform" animating on
a timer — `height: [8, 24 + Math.random() * 8, 8]` — identical for silence, a
word and a shout. The avatar never blinked, breathed or moved.

  the lips, chin displaced) plus an inner-mouth shadow. Sprites rejected
  deliberately: they need an exact mouth per avatar across 245 of them, and a
  hard-edged sprite 3% out of place looks broken where a soft band still
  reads as talking.
- FaceMotion: blink, breathing, micro-sway, gaze. Pure and delta-time driven,
  so 120Hz and a throttled tab behave identically. This is the half that
  creates the illusion — people read blink cadence long before lips.
- Expression from real agent state: thinking looks away and up, waiting holds
  eye contact, active breathes faster. Offline is frozen and desaturated on
  purpose; a breathing avatar for an agent that is not running would be the
  same class of lie as a delivery report nothing verified.

  not peak, through a noise gate and soft knee.

finite input, so every syllable above 0.36 RMS pinned the jaw open and held
it. And going offline left the blink timer at Infinity, so a face that came
back never blinked again for the whole session — both caught by tests.

Known limitation, stated rather than hidden: web-speech (the default
provider) exposes no audio stream at all, so it cannot be lip-synced. Those
calls get a synthetic envelope and the mode is reported as `synthetic`.

Calibration: per-set anchors were wrong — the women set spans an eye line
from 0.337 to 0.411, and at the wrong end the mouth shadow lands on the
chin. scripts/calibrate-avatar-rigs.mjs now measures every avatar once via

invariant to crop. Validated against hand-measured mouths: (mouthY-eyeY)/IOD

fix: verify the 5-minute inbox poll's wake, and correct the docs that hid it (v0.37.10) (#434)

3Metas retracted a message tonight and the retraction was worth more than
the claim. They called four agents deaf on a 2m19s window, then found all
four had answered at 4m22s-4m31s, clustered within 9 seconds.

That timing is the finding, and it is ours: a 5-minute poll.

Agent.checkMessages() runs every 5 minutes, and triggerMessageCheck() POSTs
a "you have N unread" prompt to the session command endpoint. sendCommand
returned success:true the instant sendKeys returned — bytes reached tmux and
nothing more. The identical unearned claim fixed in 0.37.7 for the message
wake, surviving in a SECOND implementation nobody had looked at.

It matters more than the first, not less. When a push wake stages in an
input box and never submits, this is what rescues it five minutes later —
which is precisely how the failure stayed invisible for months. Messages did
arrive; they arrived late, by a route nobody was watching.

- sendCommand takes verify:true (opt-in, so canvas/chat/meeting injection
  are unaffected) and returns submitted/staged from a real pane readback
- the poll names the mechanism in its log, so "push works" stops being an
  assumption and becomes a measurement
- CLAUDE.md and two comments in lib/agent.ts claimed polling was DISABLED by
  default. The code is `!== false` — on unless explicitly turned off. Anyone
  reading the docs would have believed there was no safety net under push.
- readback window sized deliberately (12 x 250ms) with the reasoning written
  beside it, instead of 1 second sized against nothing

3m-hr's lesson, kept verbatim in the changelog because it is the actual
point: a negative result inside a window shorter than the known response
time is not a result, it is the clock. The window could only say ABSENT,
never SLOW.

feat(agents): restore running agents after a server restart (v0.37.2) (#425)

* feat(agents): restore running agents after a server restart (v0.37.2)

A server restart left every agent offline. The intent was already recorded and
correct — persistSession() on wake means "this should be running",
unpersistSession() on hibernate means "this should stay down" — and
restoreSessions() existed. But NOTHING ever called it: zero automatic callers
in server.mjs, the startup scripts or the ecosystem config, so it had to be
triggered by hand and never was.

Three things were wrong beyond that:

1. Restore called runtime.createSession(), which opens a BARE tmux session with
   no program inside — worse than offline, because the API then shows a healthy
   session doing nothing. It now re-wakes via the wakeAgent path, relaunching
   the agent's program.

2. PersistedSession held only id/name/workingDirectory — not enough to relaunch
   faithfully. It now records program, permissionMode and sessionIndex at wake
   time, falling back to the agent's own settings for older entries.

3. Stale records were never reconciled. A record whose agent is gone from the
   registry is now dropped rather than restored as an orphan session. That is
   how 73 persisted entries accumulated against 8 real sessions.

Sleeping agents stay asleep: absence from the file IS the instruction, so no
new state was needed.

Persistence moved from ~/.ai-maestro/sessions.json to ~/.aimaestro/sessions.json,
alongside everything else. session-persistence.ts is the only reader or writer,
so nothing else is affected. The legacy file is deliberately NOT migrated — its
73 entries were stale, agentId-less and pointed at the wrong working directory,
so importing them would have made boot restore spawn dozens of wrong sessions.
It is left untouched.

Verified live: woke a throwaway agent, killed its tmux session to simulate a
machine restart, restarted the server -> "[Restore] 1 agent(s) restored, 0
already running, 0 failed" and the session came back. Then hibernated it and
restarted again -> record absent, agent stayed asleep. Existing sessions
untouched throughout; probe agent deleted afterwards.

createSession contract and were rewritten for the wake path, plus a new case
for dropping a record whose agent no longer exists.

feat(agents): agent-owned scheduled tasks (v0.37.0) (#423)

* feat(agents): agent-owned scheduled tasks (v0.36.51)

Agents are meant to be autonomous entities that can move between machines, so
their maintenance has to be theirs rather than the host's.

Schedules live at ~/.aimaestro/agents/<id>/schedule.json, beside the agent's
CozoDB, keys and canvas. Move that directory to another machine and the cadence
moves with it; whichever host runs the agent honours it, with no per-machine
setup. New agents are seeded with hourly indexing and 02:00 consolidation.

The primary trigger is the agent's OWN idle transition. The Stop hook already
reports per agent, on whichever host it runs, so when an agent goes idle the
server runs whatever that agent is due for. No host timer owns the agent, and
work lands exactly when the agent is free rather than competing with it. The
memory sweep becomes the fallback for agents that stay busy long enough to miss
an idle transition — and it runs each agent's own schedule, so the host still
holds no list of its own.

Three actions: index, consolidate, and prompt. Scheduled prompts go through the
wake chain, so a scheduled instruction gets the same proof-of-arrival as any
message — confirmed, deferred while the agent is mid-render, or queued for
retry. A schedule that fires into the void would be worse than no schedule.

Claude Code's own schedulers were evaluated and none fit: Cloud Routines get a
fresh clone with NO local file access, but the subconscious must read
~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl and the agent's local database. /loop and CronCreate
are session-scoped and in-memory ("nothing is written to disk", `durable` has
no effect), expire after 7 days, and fire only while that one session is open.
Desktop scheduled tasks persist with local access but are machine-level config,
so the schedule would not travel with the agent.

Two deliberate rules: a never-run task is due IMMEDIATELY, so an agent arriving
on a new host starts working instead of idling out a full interval; and daily
tasks use a 23-hour window rather than "today", so a machine asleep at 02:00
still consolidates when it wakes — the exact failure of the old
resident-at-2am-or-never design.

Verified live: schedule seeded and persisted to the agent's directory, `run`
indexed 24 messages, the interval correctly suppressed the next run, and
forcing a task due then firing the hook's idle transition produced
"[Schedule] 633f6cdc ran 1 task(s) on idle".

provider first, and onnxruntime-node ships CPU-only, so session creation threw

the host looked healthy while indexing nothing. macOS resolved 'auto' to CPU,

host-specific rather than as a bad default.

with a genuine CUDA-enabled onnxruntime build.

minutes, database 64 KB -> 29 MB, after months of being empty. This was never a
performance problem — nothing was slow, nothing ran at all. CPU embedding at
~7 messages/second is entirely adequate.

reports failure by RETURNING {success:false} rather than throwing, so catching
exceptions alone missed it. That is how the broken host reported "17 indexed,

1. A dead claude_dir skipped a project FOREVER. Phase 1 did
   `if (!claudeDir || !fs.existsSync(claudeDir)) continue`. Older records
   stored a nested path — <project>/<session>/subagents rather than the project
   root — and once that directory rotated away the project was skipped on every
   subsequent run, so the agent could never rediscover its own conversations.

   that no longer existed while 47 conversations sat unread in the project

fix(memory): honest subconscious status + residency-free maintenance (v0.36.45) (#417)

Follow-on to v0.36.44. Three separate reasons memory, the graph and the
subconscious "seemed to be ignored" — none of them the subsystems being broken.

1. The status endpoint STARTED what it reported on. GET
   /api/agents/[id]/subconscious called agentRegistry.getAgent(), which loads
   the agent and starts its timers; its own docstring said "This will
   initialize the agent if it doesn't exist yet." The dashboard indicator was
   therefore self-fulfilling — opening the UI made agents look active — and
   every render evicted other agents from the 10-slot LRU to draw a badge. It
   now reports the live object only when the agent is ALREADY resident, else
   reads the status.json that Agent.writeStatusFile() has been maintaining for
   exactly this purpose, with isRunning forced false: an agent absent from the
   registry is not running whatever the file last claimed. Starting stays a
   POST — an action, not an observation.

   Verified on a cold agent: reports resident:false/isRunning:false plus its
   last-active timestamp, and triggers zero agent loads.

2. Maintenance required residency. Indexing only ever needed an agent id —
   runIndexDelta opens the database itself — but ran from an Agent object's
   timer, and Agent objects live in that same 10-slot LRU. With 125 agents an
   agent was indexed only if something happened to load it, loading the 11th
   cancelled the 1st's timers, and consolidation (gated on residency at 2 AM)
   essentially never ran. lib/memory/sweep.ts walks agent directories instead:
   no hydration, no eviction, no LRU pressure. Same shape as Letta's sleep-time
   agents, where maintenance has a lifecycle independent of the primary.

3. Skills waited to be asked. Handled upstream in ai-maestro-plugins PR #29:
   memory-search, graph-query and docs-search had their descriptions rewritten
   during the v0.22.0 refactor from imperatives into keyword matchers. A skill
   description is the only thing deciding whether a model reaches for the tool,
   so agents stopped consulting memory on their own — the reported symptom
   exactly.

Adds scripts/test-memory-systems.sh, which checks what was actually wrong
rather than liveness: id determinism, how many databases were written this
week, whether search returns results, whether the graph is populated, whether
querying status changes status, and whether maintenance can run off the LRU.

separating "never indexed" from "indexed an hour ago, since evicted".

fix(memory): deterministic message IDs — agent memory was 8x duplicated (v0.36.44) (#416)

Investigating why agents "seem to ignore" memory and the graph led to 36 GB of
duplicated data and a one-line cause.

msgId.message() built `msg-{ts}-{Math.random()}`. `:put messages` upserts on
msg_id, so a random component guaranteed an INSERT rather than an update.
Every re-index stored another copy of the message, its ~26 msg_terms rows and
its ~1.5 KB embedding. index-delta assumes indexing is idempotent; it never

feat(delivery): persist hook status to close the idle-gate blind spot (v0.36.42) (#414)

v0.36.40 gated pane wakes on whether the agent was busy, but the only signal
available was sessionActivity — written by the PTY layer, which runs only while
someone has the terminal open. So the gate worked for agents being watched and
was inert for every other agent in the fleet. That was shipped documented
rather than hidden, and this closes it.

The Claude Code hook already knew the answer. It fires on Stop / SessionStart /
Notification and reports the agent's real state, but broadcastActivityUpdate()
only pushed that to WebSocket subscribers and dropped it on the floor. It now
lands in shared-state.hookStatus (sessionName -> {status, notificationType,
at}), and lib/session-idle prefers it over PTY recency. This is the only
busy/idle signal that exists for an agent with no attached terminal.

Two other candidates were measured and rejected before landing on this, and are
recorded in session-idle so nobody re-tries them: tmux #{session_activity} was
25 minutes stale on an agent that was visibly mid-turn, and diffing two pane
captures 600ms apart was backwards in both directions — identical while
working, different while idle.

SAFETY. The two possible mistakes are not symmetric. Deferring a genuinely idle
agent delays a wake by one tick; typing into a permission_request ANSWERS THE
MODAL. So the mapping is deliberately conservative: only states positively
recognised as waiting count as idle — 'idle', and 'waiting_for_input' only when
notificationType is 'idle_prompt'. 'active', 'permission_request' and anything
unrecognised defer. A future hook state we do not know about will defer, not
type into it.

Hook reports expire after 15 minutes. An agent that dies mid-turn would
otherwise leave 'active' as its last word forever and permanently block its own
wakes; after the TTL we fall back to PTY recency.

Also fixed, found while verifying this rather than by a user:
/api/messages/pending-wakes was returning a BUILD-TIME SNAPSHOT. The handler
reads only in-memory maps and calls no dynamic API, so Next statically
prerendered it and served frozen zeros — an endpoint whose entire job is
reporting live state reported nothing since it shipped in 0.36.41. Now
force-dynamic, with a comment saying why it must stay that way.

hookStatus is added to BOTH shared-state.ts and shared-state-bridge.mjs with
late-init guards, since either module graph may initialise _sharedState first,
and session-idle reads it optionally so a missing map degrades to the PTY
signal instead of throwing inside a wake.

Verified: synthetic POSTs matching the hook's exact payload produce
idle=true/source=hook for 'idle' and idle=false for 'permission_request'; the
real hook binary writes the correct state for the right cwd; the hook is wired
for all three events in ~/.claude/settings.json.

feat(delivery): wake-adapter chain, idle gating, and retry (v0.36.39–v0.36.41) (#413)

* feat(delivery): explicit wake-adapter chain with per-route proof (v0.36.39)

deliver() woke agents through an implicit if-chain: push to a streaming
session, push to a channel, then maybe send-keys, with the decision to skip
the fallback buried in a boolean. It worked, but nothing in the shape of the
code said which routes were alternatives, what order they belonged in, or what
each one could actually prove — so the v0.36.37 bug (an unproven channel push
suppressing the pane fallback) was easy to write and hard to see.

Make the chain explicit. Each route is a WakeAdapter that reports one of four
statuses instead of a boolean:

  confirmed   — something downstream of the transport proved arrival
  sent        — handed off successfully; arrival unknown
  unavailable — route does not apply to this agent
  failed      — route applies and did not work

Only `confirmed` stops the chain. That single rule generalises the fix: a
`sent` outcome must never suppress the next route, because an unproven wake is
worth nothing to an agent that is waiting on it.

Order is stream → channel → pane: strongest proof first, universal fallback
last. stream is an in-process handoff into a live SDK input stream with no
transport to lose it. channel is `sent` on push and `confirmed` only after the
session acks. pane needs no cooperation from whatever occupies it, so it covers
Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider and a bare shell — it is the floor the
chain falls back to, never a route it depends on.

WebSocket and webhook stay OUTSIDE the chain and keep firing unconditionally.
ws.send() carries no application-level ack and its clients are dashboards and
AMP libraries rather than the agent's loop, so counting it as a wake would be
the same overclaiming this work exists to prevent. Folding in the webhook would
have stopped it firing for agents that also have a channel, silently breaking
integrations.

Behaviour change: a confirmed stream push now skips channel and pane. Those are
different runtimes (an SDK session is not a CLI in a pane), so this removes
redundant work rather than a route — but it is a change worth knowing for any
hybrid agent.

DeliveryResult gains verifiedBy and wakeAttempts (the full ordered record),
which is the substrate the undelivered-message surface will build on. Logs now
read `stream:unavailable → channel:sent → pane:confirmed`; a wholly unconfirmed
wake logs at warn with the same trace.

mapping, a throwing adapter not stranding the chain, and end-to-end fall-through
from an unverified channel to the pane.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(delivery): idle-gate pane wakes instead of typing into a busy TUI (v0.36.40)

Typing into a pane that is mid-render is where notifications get eaten: the
text lands in a screen being repainted and vanishes. That is the dropped-Enter
the fleet has fought for months, and sending harder cannot fix it — the send is
not what fails, the timing is.

So stop sending at bad moments. The pane adapter now checks whether the session
is idle; if it is busy the wake is queued and flushed on the idle transition.
Same trade Claude Code makes for its own peer messaging, where events queue and
drain at the receiver's next turn and the docs explicitly say not to poll or
nag instead.

Only the PANE route is gated. The streaming and channel routes hand off into
queues their runtimes drain safely at a turn boundary, so they are unaffected
by TUI render state and are never deferred.

A queued wake has NOT been delivered, so it gets its own status rather than
being folded into `sent`. WakeStatus gains `deferred`, WakeResult gains a
`deferred` flag, and `notified` stays false for it. The inbox write already
happened, so deferral is a delay rather than a loss — but it must never be
counted as an arrival. That is the same rule the rest of this subsystem runs
on, applied to a new state.

lib/wake-queue.ts holds the per-agent FIFO. It self-starts a 5s unref'd ticker
on first enqueue and stops when empty, flushes one wake per agent per tick
(a burst into a pane that just went idle is its own mistimed interruption),
expires entries after 10 minutes rather than interrupting long after the fact,
and caps each agent at 20 by dropping the OLDEST — recent context wins, and
every dropped or expired message is still in the inbox.

Idle detection was private to sessions-service, so extract it to
lib/session-idle.ts: one source of truth for the 30s threshold, and the wake
path can ask the question without importing the session service graph. A
session we have never seen output from counts as idle — it is freshly attached
or at a prompt, and there is nothing to interrupt.

one-per-tick ordering, TTL expiry, cap eviction, a throwing flush not losing
the rest of the queue, and that a deferred wake is never reported as notified.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(delivery): retry unconfirmed wakes + operator surface (v0.36.41)

An unconfirmed wake used to be the end of the story: deliver() logged a warning
and moved on, so a message could sit in an inbox forever with nothing anywhere
saying the agent had never been shown it.

Retry reuses the idle queue rather than adding a second subsystem. The queue
now holds two kinds of pending wake — 'busy' (never attempted, pane was
mid-render) and 'unconfirmed' (attempted, nothing could prove it landed) — and
both want the same thing: try again when the agent is quiet. Unconfirmed
attempts re-enter with a backoff (0s/30s/2m/10m) and are bounded: after four
attempts we give up LOUDLY. A notification that has failed four times is not
going to start working, and retyping into the pane every ten minutes is worse
than stopping. The message is in the inbox either way.

Surface: GET /api/messages/pending-wakes lists every message that is on disk
but unproven, with reason, attempt count and retry timer. DeliveryResult gained
verified/verifiedBy/deferred/wakeAttempts, and those are now threaded through
sendFromUI → messages-service → the API, which previously dropped them — so
callers could not tell "accepted" from "proved" even though deliver() knew.

scripts/test-message-wake.sh answers "how do I test this?" end to end: send a
real AMP message to a live local agent and assert whether anything could prove
it landed. Verified in production against 23blocks-iac, where the trace read
`stream:unavailable → channel:sent → pane:confirmed` — the original bug being
caught and survived live, on a real agent with a registered-but-unacked channel.

KNOWN GAP, documented in lib/session-idle.ts rather than papered over: the idle
gate only has a signal while a PTY is attached, so it engages for agents someone
is watching and is inert for the rest. Two alternatives were measured and
rejected, not assumed — tmux #{session_activity} was 25 minutes stale on a
visibly working agent, and diffing pane captures 600ms apart was backwards in
both directions (identical while working, different while idle). The real fix is
to persist the status the Claude Code hook already reports on Stop /
Notification(idle_prompt), which today is broadcast and never stored.

fix(delivery): never report a message wake we cannot prove (v0.36.37) (#411)

* fix(delivery): never report a message wake we cannot prove (v0.36.37)

Both wake paths reported deliveries that had not happened, and the channel
path used that false positive to suppress its own fallback.

Channels: pushToChannel() returning true only means our local HTTP server
accepted the POST and mcp.notification() wrote to the stdio transport. Claude
Code never acknowledges channel notifications and drops them SILENTLY when the
session did not register the server as a channel (no --channels, plugin off the
Anthropic allowlist, or channelsEnabled unset). deliver() treated that as proof
and skipped the tmux fallback, so in exactly the configuration a fleet rollout
starts from, the message vanished with no delivery at all.

The failure is static per session, so one confirmation covers its lifetime.
The channel server now exposes an amp_channel_ack tool and persists
verified:true into ~/.aimaestro/channels/<agentId>.json; only isChannelVerified()
may suppress the fallback. Until a session confirms, both paths fire — a
duplicate nudge is cheap, a lost message is not. If the model never calls the
tool we degrade to today's behaviour rather than to silence.

tmux: sendTmuxNotification() returned void, so notified:true meant only "two
send-keys calls did not throw". It now reads the pane back and looks for a
per-message ref, polling for render lag before resending, and reports
honestly: verified (read back), notified-but-unverified (runtime offers no
capture), or not notified (pane readable, message never arrived).

Readback needs no cooperation from whatever occupies the pane, so it is the
runtime-agnostic equivalent of the channel ack and covers Claude Code, Codex,
Gemini CLI, Aider or a bare shell alike. This matters because channels cannot
carry the fleet: --channels only accepts Anthropic-allowlisted plugins unless
an admin sets allowedChannelPlugins, which is Team/Enterprise only.

The pane notification now also carries the message body, single-lined and
truncated, instead of a "check your inbox" pointer the agent could ignore.
Single-lining is required, not cosmetic: a raw newline in send-keys submits a
TUI early and opens an unterminated quote at a shell prompt.
NOTIFICATION_FORMAT still owns the header line, so custom templates keep
working.

DeliveryResult.verified exposes the distinction to callers: notified without
verified means sent-unconfirmed and must not be read as proof.

Cost: the fallback path now takes ~400ms when confirmed and is bounded at
~2.3s when the message never lands.

fix: tmux-scroll capability handshake — no more JSON typed into old-host prompts (v0.35.59)

Remote hosts and containers on older versions don't understand the new
tmux-scroll frame, and old servers write unknown WS messages straight into
the PTY — so scrolling typed literal {"type":"tmux-scroll",...} into the
agent's prompt. Now:
- Server sends {type:'server-caps', tmuxScroll:true} on terminal connect.
  The frame tunnels through proxies, so clients learn the END server's
  capability (old hosts never send it).
- Client (wheel + touch) forwards tmux-scroll only after caps arrive;
  otherwise it falls back to local xterm scrolling (pre-v0.35.56 behavior).
  Caps reset on every reconnect.
- Hardening: this server now DROPS unknown typed protocol frames instead of
  writing them to the PTY, so the next new frame type can't reproduce this.

fix: remote chat race condition and agentId mismatch (v0.35.4)

Two bugs prevented chat from working on remote hosts:

1. Race condition: handleRemoteWorker registered the client message
   handler inside workerWs.on('open'), but the client sends
   chat:requestHistory immediately on connect — before the remote
   WebSocket connects. Messages were silently lost. Fix: register
   clientWs.on('message') immediately with a queue that flushes
   when the remote connects.

2. agentId mismatch: getChatHistory and startJsonlWatcher used the
   local server's agentId to look up the agent on the remote host,
   where it doesn't exist. Fix: fall back to sessionName lookup

fix: recover from WebGL context loss on Mac Mini

fix: recover from WebGL context loss on Mac Mini (#278)

The Mac Mini's GPU triggers WebGL context loss, leaving xterm.js's
internal renderer undefined. RenderService.dimensions uses an unsafe
non-null assertion that crashes with "Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading 'dimensions')" on any scrollToBottom/fit call.

Root cause: onContextLoss disposed the WebGL addon but only called
refresh(), which silently no-ops when _renderer.value is undefined.
The terminal was left in an unrecoverable state with no renderer.

Fix: Re-open the terminal element after WebGL disposal, forcing
xterm.js to create a new canvas renderer. Also wrap scrollToBottom
in try-catch as a safety net during the brief recovery window.

Closes #278

fix(cli): consolidate agent resolvers, fix HOST_URLS crash, fix BSD sed (v0.21.25)

Fixes #190 — HOST_URLS: unbound variable crash in messaging-helper.sh

## Problem

Three separate agent resolution code paths had diverged:

1. `resolve_agent` in messaging-helper.sh — multi-host only, referenced
   deleted HOST_URLS array causing unbound variable crash
2. `resolve_agent_simple` in agent-helper.sh — local-only fallback
3. Inline resolution in cmd_show (aimaestro-agent.sh) — duplicate code

Additionally:
- localhost was not searched when hosts.json only had remote/Tailscale entries
- bump-version.sh used BSD-only `sed -i ''` syntax, breaking on Linux
- No input sanitization on the @host part of agent@host syntax

## Solution

### Unified resolve_agent (agent-helper.sh)

Single resolver replaces all three with a three-phase strategy:
- Phase 1: If @host specified → query that specific host
- Phase 2: Try local /api/agents first (fast, covers 99% of CLI use)
- Phase 3: Fall back to multi-host search via search_agent_all_hosts()

Sets all globals needed by both CLI and messaging functions:
RESOLVED_AGENT_ID, RESOLVED_ALIAS, RESOLVED_HOST_ID, RESOLVED_HOST_URL,
RESOLVED_NAME.

### Localhost auto-injection (messaging-helper.sh)

search_agent_all_hosts() now always probes and includes localhost:23000
in the search list, even when hosts.json only contains remote entries.

### Input sanitization

Both agent and host parts are validated before use in URLs/commands:
- Agent: ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$
- Host: ^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$

### BSD sed fix (bump-version.sh)

Replaced `sed -i ''` with portable `sed -i.bak` + rm pattern.
Added early exit when target version matches current version.

### cmd_show cleanup (aimaestro-agent.sh)

Replaced 35 lines of inline duplicate resolution code with a single
resolve_agent() call.

## Files changed

- plugin/scripts/agent-helper.sh — unified resolve_agent, removed
  resolve_agent_simple and conditional override
- plugin/scripts/messaging-helper.sh — removed resolve_agent (moved to
  agent-helper.sh), added localhost injection to search_agent_all_hosts
- plugin/scripts/aimaestro-agent.sh — cmd_show uses unified resolver

perf(subconscious): eliminate resource waste in delta indexing (v0.21.24)

perf(subconscious): eliminate resource waste in delta indexing (v0.21.24)

5 optimizations that dramatically reduce memory, CPU, and TCP overhead:

1. File-size delta detection: Use fs.statSync().size to skip unchanged files
   without reading them. Previously every cycle read entire .jsonl files
   just to count lines.

2. Direct function call: maintainMemory() now calls runIndexDelta() directly
   instead of HTTP self-fetch to localhost. Eliminates TCP connection,
   HTTP parsing, and JSON serialization per agent per cycle.

3. Global project discovery cache: ~/.claude/projects/ scan results cached
   with 10-min TTL. Previously each of ~108 agents independently scanned
   and read the first 20 lines of every .jsonl file.

4. Single-read pipeline: Conversations needing indexing are read once.
   Previously each file was read 3 times (filter, dry-run, index).

5. Extracted lib/index-delta.ts: Core logic extracted from API route into
   a module callable both directly and via HTTP. API route is now a thin
   wrapper.

fix(terminal): resolve copy/paste and text selection issues (#161)

* fix(terminal): resolve copy/paste and selection breaking after terminal writes

Root causes:
- MutationObserver on terminal container created a DOM mutation feedback loop
  on every terminal.write(), disrupting xterm.js rendering and selection
- CSS display:none on accessibility tree broke xterm.js internal DOM structure
- userSelect:none on container cascaded to xterm.js helper textarea, blocking
  clipboard operations
- Redundant onMouseDown focus handler interfered with xterm.js selection init
- WebGL loaded via separate useEffect caused race condition on agent switch
  (cached import resolved instantly, switching renderer before selection stabilized)

Fixes:
- Remove MutationObserver entirely; use CSS-only approach for accessibility tree
- Replace display:none with pointer-events:none + visually-hidden pattern
- Remove userSelect:none and onMouseDown handler from terminal containers
- Load WebGL inline during initializeTerminal() instead of via separate effect
- Remove TerminalViewNew (subset of TerminalView with no unique features)

fix: PTY handle leak prevents new terminal sessions (#104)

fix: PTY handle leak prevents new terminal sessions (#104)

Root cause: WebSocket error handler didn't trigger PTY cleanup, and
there was no periodic cleanup for orphaned sessions.

Fixes (based on node-pty best practices from GitHub issues #333, #382):

1. Use `ptyProcess.kill()` instead of `process.kill(-pid)`
   - node-pty's kill() properly handles underlying PTY cleanup
   - Process group kill (-pid) is unreliable with node-pty

2. Added `alreadyExited` flag to prevent killing dead processes
   - Calling pty.kill() on dead process throws error (issue #333)
   - onExit handler now passes ptyAlreadyExited=true

3. Added `cleanedUp` flag to prevent double cleanup
   - Multiple code paths could trigger cleanup simultaneously

4. Fixed `ws.on('error')` to trigger client disconnect handling
   - Previously only logged, now properly cleans up

5. Added periodic orphaned PTY cleanup (every 5 minutes)
   - Catches sessions with no clients and no pending cleanup timer

6. Added `/api/debug/pty` monitoring endpoint
   - Shows system PTY usage vs limit
   - Reports health status (healthy/warning/critical at 60%/80%)

Sources:
- https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty/issues/333
- https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty/issues/382

Fixes #104

- Each agent with CozoDB database = ~25MB
- 68 agents × 25MB = ~1.7GB permanent memory usage
- Agents were NEVER unloaded, causing PM2 restarts at 2GB limit

- Max 10 agents in memory at once (configurable)
- Least recently used agents are properly evicted (including CozoDB shutdown)
- Memory now capped at ~250MB instead of 1.7GB

- AgentSubconscious writes status files to ~/.aimaestro/agents/{id}/status.json
- /api/subconscious reads from files instead of loading agents
- Status files marked as stale after 10 minutes (agent likely stopped)

This commit addresses critical performance and behavior issues caused by the tab-based
architecture where all session components are mounted simultaneously.

Key Fixes:

1. Agent Registration Endpoint Enhancement (app/api/agents/register/route.ts)
   - Added support for simple sessionName + workingDirectory registration format
   - Maintains backward compatibility with full agent config format
   - Enables WorkTree to register agents on-demand without validation errors

   - Created server-side proxy endpoint to avoid CORS issues
   - Uses native Node.js http/https modules for reliable health checks
   - Updated HostsSettings.tsx and HostsSection.tsx to use proxy endpoint
   - Fixes "Failed to fetch" browser errors when checking remote hosts

3. AI Search Conversation Filtering (lib/rag/search.ts, app/api/agents/[id]/search/route.ts)
   - Added conversationFile parameter support across all search modes
   - Enables accurate filtering of search results within specific conversations
   - Applied to hybrid, semantic, term, and symbol search functions

4. WorkTree Lazy-Loading (components/WorkTree.tsx, app/page.tsx)
   - Added isVisible prop to prevent initialization on mount
   - Only fetches data when user actually views WorkTree tab
   - Prevents mass agent registration for all sessions on page load
   - Uses hasInitialized state to ensure single initialization per session

5. MessageCenter Lazy-Loading (components/MessageCenter.tsx, app/page.tsx)
   - Added isVisible prop with lazy initialization
   - Only fetches messages and starts polling when tab becomes visible
   - Prevents unnecessary API calls for hidden message tabs
   - Stops 10-second polling intervals for non-visible sessions

Root Cause:
The tab-based multi-terminal architecture mounts all sessions simultaneously
using CSS visibility toggling. This caused WorkTree and MessageCenter to
initialize for every session on page load, leading to:
- Mass agent registration requests (400 errors)
- Excessive message fetching API calls
- Multiple polling intervals running simultaneously
- CORS errors from direct browser requests to remote hosts

Impact:
- Eliminates browser "Failed to fetch" errors
- Prevents 400 "Missing required fields" registration errors
- Reduces initial page load API calls by ~90%
- Improves overall application performance and user experience

- No progress updates, but no duplication either

- Won't see progress bars or status updates
- Will only see final results

Fix critical PTY leak bug causing system resource exhaustion (v0.4.0)

Fix critical PTY leak bug causing system resource exhaustion (v0.4.0)

CRITICAL BUG FIXED: PTY processes were never cleaned up on client disconnect

## Problem
AI Maestro was leaking PTY processes every time a browser refreshed or reconnected
to a session. Over 11 hours of operation, this accumulated 615+ orphaned PTY
processes, exhausting the system's PTY limit (default: 511 on macOS).

Symptoms:
- "Device not configured" errors when creating new terminal sessions
- "[forkpty: Device not configured]" errors in tmux
- PTY count growing continuously from 41 → 656+ processes
- Unable to create new tmux sessions or terminal windows

Root cause:
The WebSocket 'close' event handler removed clients from the session but never
killed the underlying PTY process. Each browser refresh/reconnect created a new
PTY that stayed alive forever.

## Solution
Implemented 30-second grace period cleanup:
- When last client disconnects, schedule cleanup timer (30s)
- If client reconnects within 30s, cancel cleanup (reuse same PTY)
- If no reconnection after 30s, kill PTY process and cleanup session
- Preserves UX for quick reconnections while preventing resource leaks

Changes in server.mjs:
1. Added cleanupTimer to sessionState (line 95)
2. Cancel cleanup on client reconnect (lines 184-189)
3. Schedule cleanup on disconnect if no clients remain (lines 277-313)

Verification:
- Before fix: 656 PTYs after 11 hours
- After stopping AI Maestro: PTYs dropped to 41
- After fix: PTYs remain stable at ~41 even with frequent reconnections

Fix selection reverting to yellow after new content arrives

Selection worked initially but turned yellow again when terminal received new content.

**Root cause:**
- xterm.js selection layer gets invalidated when terminal content updates
- After write(), the selection layer needs refresh() to re-render properly
- Without refresh, browser's default yellow selection shows through

**Solution:**
- Added debounced refresh after every terminal.write()
- Waits 200ms after last content update before refreshing
- Prevents performance issues during rapid output (e.g., large file dumps)
- Only refreshes visible portion (rows 0 to terminal.rows-1)

**How it works:**
1. Terminal receives data → write(data)
2. Clear any pending refresh timeout
3. Set new timeout for 200ms
4. If more data arrives → reset timeout (debounce)
5. After 200ms of silence → refresh() → selection layer re-renders with theme colors

**Performance:**
- Debouncing prevents excessive refresh() calls during rapid output
- Only refreshes visible rows (not entire scrollback buffer)
- 200ms delay is imperceptible to users but prevents thrashing

Fixes reported issue: "it works when I change to a session and select.
then if I receive more content to the console, is yellow again."

Fix mobile/desktop interference with key prop isolation

Mobile and desktop dashboards were interfering with each other during resize.

**Root cause:**
- During React re-render when switching layouts, both dashboards briefly exist
- Both render ALL sessions (tab architecture)
- Each session creates duplicate WebSocket connections and terminal instances
- Multiple TerminalViews try to write to same PTY simultaneously
- Race conditions cause session refreshing issues

**Solution:**
- Added unique `key` props to TerminalProvider for each layout
- `key="mobile-dashboard"` for mobile layout
- `key="desktop-dashboard"` for desktop layout
- React now completely unmounts old layout before mounting new one
- Ensures only ONE set of WebSocket connections exists at a time
- Eliminates race conditions and state conflicts

**How it works:**
When isMobile changes, React sees different key → triggers full unmount/mount cycle:
1. Old layout unmounts → all WebSockets close, terminals dispose
2. New layout mounts → fresh WebSockets, fresh terminals
3. Zero overlap, zero interference

Fixes reported issue: "when I am using the mobile and the desktop is open,
they interfere between each other. like the session refreshing"
